```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(appauth)
```

The package contains what must be identical across all applications: passwords, login protection, sessions, blocking, and permission checks. Everything that differs between applications is plugged in through extension points. This document describes each of them.

| Point | Purpose | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permission source | How the application decides what a role or user may do | `aa_can()`, `aa_require()`, `aa_register_module()` |
| Roles | Which roles exist and which one is the administrator | `aa_settings(roles, admin_role)` |
| Event hook | Where to write the log, what to notify about | `on_event` in all modules |
| Card slots | A custom block in the user card | `aa_users_server(extra_card_ui, extra_card_server)` |
| Texts | Language and wording | `aa_texts()` |
| Appearance | Colors, light theme, title, logo | `aa_app_head()`, `aa_auth_server(title, logo)` |
| Security parameters | Timeouts, limits, auto-login | `aa_settings()` |

# Permissions

## The "permission -> roles" matrix

The format follows a typical application config: a permission name and the roles it is available to (a vector or a single string).

```{r}
provider <- aa_permissions_from_matrix(list(
  Tasks  = c("admin", "user", "viewer"),
  Run    = c("admin", "user"),
  Access = "admin"
))

provider(list(login = "ivan", role = "user"))
aa_can(list(login = "ivan", role = "user"), "Run", provider)
aa_can(list(login = "ivan", role = "user"), "Access", provider)
```

Name permissions however you like: `"Tasks"`, `"Run"`, `"export"`. The package does not know them. The administrator role does **not** get permissions by itself: if needed, list it in the matrix.

### A matrix that changes on the fly

If the application has a permission editor and the matrix changes without a restart, pass a function. It is read on every check:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
provider <- aa_permissions_from_matrix(function() conf_rv()$access_matrix)
```

## A custom permission source

Any `function(user)` that returns a vector of the user's permission names will do. This is how you implement per-user permissions from a database, by group, or from an external system:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
provider <- function(user) {
  if (identical(user$role, "owner")) {
    return(c("reports", "export", "users"))     # the owner can do everything
  }

  DBI::dbGetQuery(
    conn, "SELECT permission FROM user_permissions WHERE login = ?",
    params = list(user$login)
  )$permission
}
```

`aa_can()` is closed by default: if the function fails, returns non-strings, or returns `NA`, the permission is denied. A working example is in `examples/custom-permissions-app`.

## Where to check a permission

* **In the UI**: `aa_can(user, "Run", provider)` decides whether to show a button or a tab. This is a convenience, not protection.
* **On the server in every handler**: `aa_require(auth, "Run", provider, on_event = ...)` as the first line. Without the permission the handler stops silently, the user sees a notification, and the hook receives `access_denied`.
* **When registering modules**: `aa_register_module(auth, "Access", provider, function() mod_server(...))` attaches the server part of a tab only for those who have the permission.

# Roles

```{r}
settings <- aa_settings(
  roles = c("owner", "editor", "viewer"),
  admin_role = "owner"
)
settings$roles
```

`admin_role` must be one of `roles`. Only this role manages users (the `aa_users_server()` module checks it on the server and verifies it against the database on every action, regardless of your matrix). The first administrator created also gets this role.

# Events

The package writes nothing to the application logs: for each event it calls the function `on_event(event, user, session_id, value)`, one for all modules.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
log_event <- function(event, user, session_id, value) {
  write_action_log(user = user, func = event, session_id = session_id, value = value)
}

aa_auth_server("auth", conn, settings, on_event = log_event)
aa_users_server("users", conn, auth, settings, on_event = log_event)
aa_require(auth, "Run", provider, on_event = log_event)
```

The hook receives:

* `event`: the event key from the catalog;
* `user`: the login the event is attributed to (for a failed login this is the entered login, or `"anonymous"` if there is no login);
* `session_id`: the Shiny session identifier;
* `value`: a detail (see the catalog), always a string. Passwords and tokens never appear in events.

An error inside the hook never interrupts a package action: it is printed as a message, for example `appauth: session closed: ann (token_revoked)`.

The event catalog (returned by `aa_events()`):

```{r}
knitr::kable(aa_events())
```

The hook can be used for more than logging: for example, to send a Telegram notification on `login_locked` or `user_blocked`. The hook can also receive the application's own events from your code; the package does not validate the names.

## A ready-made handler for the log

To avoid writing the hook by hand, build it with `aa_event_logger()`: you supply only the writer function `writer(action, user, session_id, value)`, while event filtering, the action names of your log, enabling of logging, and value conversion are handled by the package.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_log <- function(action, user, session_id, value) {
  # write to your table, file, or Telegram
}

log_event <- aa_event_logger(
  write_log,
  # which events to write and under which names (without actions, all events are written under their keys)
  actions = c(login_failed = "Login failed", user_added = "User add", user_removed = "User delete"),
  # a switch from the config: the function is called on every event, changes take effect immediately
  enabled = function(event) isTRUE(conf_rv()$logging$action_log),
  # for example, older logs stored only the login in value
  format_value = function(event, user, value) sub(" \\(.*\\)$", "", value)
)

auth <- aa_auth_server("auth", conn, settings, on_event = log_event)
```

Event names are validated immediately: a typo in `actions` or `events` raises an error when the handler is created instead of silently skipping the event. A failure in `writer` does not interrupt a package action; it is printed as a message.

# User card slots

The user card (double-click on a row) shows the standard actions. A custom block is added with two functions:

* `extra_card_ui(login, ns)` returns the block's UI; wrap identifiers in `ns()`;
* `extra_card_server(input, output, session, login)` is called **once** when the module starts, inside its namespace; `login` is a reactive value with the login of the open card.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
card_ui <- function(login, ns) {
  div(
    class = "aa-card-section",
    h5("Permissions"),
    checkboxGroupInput(ns("permissions"), NULL, choices = c("reports", "export")),
    actionButton(ns("save_permissions"), "Save")
  )
}

card_server <- function(input, output, session, login) {
  observeEvent(input$save_permissions, {
    # take the role from server state, not from input
    req(identical(isolate(auth$user())$role, "owner"), login())
    save_permissions(login(), input$permissions)
  })
}

aa_users_server("users", conn, auth, settings,
                extra_card_ui = card_ui, extra_card_server = card_server)
```

The slot handler must check the permission for the action itself: the slot is your code, and the package is not responsible for it. The `aa-card-section` class gives the block the standard styling.

Build the rest of the "Access" tab content (the role permission editor, log switches) yourself:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tabPanel("Access", aa_users_ui("users"), my_permissions_editor(), my_log_switches())
```

# Account area: buttons next to the user badge

Changing your own password and signing out on all devices are ordinary application buttons connected to package functions. It is convenient to keep them next to the user badge and the "Sign out" button:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# server: the password change module is attached once
pw <- aa_password_server("password", conn, auth, settings, on_event = log_event)

# UI: the user badge and buttons
div(
  span(icon("user"), user$login, paste0(" (", user$role, ")")),
  actionButton("change_password", "Change password"),
  actionButton("logout_all", "Sign out on all devices"),
  actionButton("logout", "Sign out")
)

# password change: the module form in a dialog, closed after a successful change
observeEvent(input$change_password, {
  showModal(modalDialog(aa_password_ui("password"), title = "Change password",
                        easyClose = TRUE, footer = modalButton("Close")))
})
observeEvent(pw$changed(), removeModal(), ignoreInit = TRUE)

# sign out everywhere only after confirmation: the button also kicks out other devices
observeEvent(input$logout_all, {
  showModal(modalDialog(
    "All your sessions on all devices will be ended.",
    title = "Sign out on all devices?", easyClose = TRUE,
    footer = tagList(modalButton("Cancel"),
                     actionButton("logout_all_confirm", "Sign out everywhere", class = "btn-danger"))
  ))
})
observeEvent(input$logout_all_confirm, {
  removeModal()
  auth$logout_all(reload = TRUE)
})

observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout(reload = TRUE))
```

What happens:

* `aa_password_server()` checks the current password, rejects the same and weak passwords, revokes the tokens of the other sessions and keeps the current one; event `password_changed`.
* `auth$logout_all()` revokes all of the user's tokens and signs out immediately; events `sessions_revoked` (the value is the login) and `logout`. Open sessions on other devices are closed by `aa_session_guard()` at its next check (within 30 seconds by default), so the guard must be attached.
* If auto-login is disabled (`autologin = FALSE`), sessions have no tokens: "sign out everywhere" closes only the current session. Such a setup needs your own session storage.

A working example: `examples/minimal-app`.

# Password recovery by email

Disabled by default. Enabling it takes three things: a function that sends the email, the application address for the link, and user email addresses.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(emayili)

# sending function: the package does not send emails itself, it only supplies the address and the link
send_reset <- function(email, link, login) {
  msg <- envelope() %>%
    from("My App <noreply@example.com>") %>%
    to(email) %>%
    subject("Password recovery") %>%
    html(paste0(
      "<p>Hello, ", htmltools::htmlEscape(login), "!</p>",
      "<p>To set a new password, follow this <a href='", link, "'>link</a>. ",
      "It is valid for 60 minutes and works only once.</p>",
      "<p>If you did not request recovery, just ignore this email.</p>"
    ))

  smtp <- gmail(Sys.getenv("APP_EMAIL"), Sys.getenv("APP_EMAIL_PWD"))
  smtp(msg)
}

settings <- aa_settings(
  reset_enabled  = TRUE,
  send_reset     = send_reset,
  reset_base_url = "https://apps.example.com/my_app"   # the application address as users see it
)
```

Nothing else needs to be attached: `aa_auth_server()` shows the "Forgot your password?" link itself, reads the `reset` parameter from the address, shows the new password form, and reports the events `password_reset_requested`, `password_reset_done`, and `password_reset_failed`.

* **User addresses** are set by the administrator in the user card (the "Email for password recovery" block) or when adding a user; programmatically this is `aa_set_email()` and the `email` argument of `aa_create_user()`. Without an address no email is sent, and the user is left with a password reset by the administrator.
* **The response to the user is always the same**: whether the user was found, whether they have an address, and whether the limit was exceeded is visible only in the `password_reset_requested` event (`value` holds the reason: `sent`, `no_user`, `no_email`, `blocked`, `throttled`, `send_failed`).
* **`reset_base_url`** must point to the application the way users open it, including the nginx prefix and over HTTPS. `/?reset=<token>` is appended to it.
* **The `send_reset` function** runs in the user's session, so a slow send delays the response. If an error is thrown, the user will not see it, but the reason (`send_failed`) goes to the event and the application log.
* **Limits**: `reset_max_per_hour` emails per user and `reset_max_per_minute` for the whole application; excess requests are silently ignored.
* **Custom UI**: the logic is available without the module as `aa_request_password_reset()`, `aa_reset_token_login()`, and `aa_reset_password_with_token()`.

The form texts are changed with the `forgot_*`, `reset_*`, and `email_*` keys (`aa_text_keys()`).

# Two-factor authentication (TOTP)

Disabled by default and **voluntary**: users enable protection themselves, and those who have it enabled enter a code at login. You need a secret encryption key and an account area block:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
settings <- aa_settings(
  totp_enabled = TRUE,
  totp_key     = Sys.getenv("APP_TOTP_KEY"),   # a string of at least 16 characters, kept outside the database and the repository
  totp_issuer  = "Reports portal"              # the name the authenticator app will show
)

# server: the module is attached once (like password change)
aa_totp_server("totp", conn, auth, settings, on_event = log_event)

# UI: a block in the profile
tabPanel("Profile", aa_password_ui("password"), hr(), aa_totp_ui("totp"))
```

Nothing else needs to be attached: `aa_auth_server()` asks for the code itself after a correct password if the user has protection enabled.

* **Setup**: the "Enable" button shows a QR code (if the optional `qrcode` package is installed) and a key for manual entry; after a correct code the protection is enabled, and the user is shown 10 recovery codes once. The user's other sessions are ended at that point.
* **Login**: a code from the app (6 digits) or a recovery code. A code from the app is accepted once; wrong codes count as failed login attempts and lock the login just like password guessing. Auto-login by cookie does not ask for a code.
* **Disabling** requires the password and a code. **Lost phone**: a recovery code or a 2FA reset by the administrator in the user card (event `totp_reset`).
* **The `totp_key` key** encrypts secrets in the database. If it is lost or replaced, the secrets become unreadable, and users will have to set up 2FA again (reset by the administrator). Store the key separately from the database and backups.
* **Events**: `totp_enabled`, `totp_disabled`, `totp_failed`, `totp_reset`, `recovery_code_used`.
* **Custom logic without modules**: `aa_totp_setup()`, `aa_totp_enable()`, `aa_verify_second_factor()`, `aa_totp_disable()`, `aa_totp_enabled()`, `aa_recovery_codes_left()`. Call `aa_login_gate()` before `aa_verify_second_factor()`, and `aa_record_attempt()` after a wrong code, otherwise the code can be guessed.
* **Tests**: the code for the current step is computed by `aa_totp_code(secret)`; a repeat of an already accepted code is rejected, so in a test for a second login take the code of the next step (`aa_totp_code(secret, Sys.time() + 30)`).

The form texts are changed with the `totp_*` keys and `card_totp` (`aa_text_keys()`).

# Sign-in with Google

Sign-in with Google (OpenID Connect) is enabled through settings and creates nothing by itself: only a user who already exists in the database and has an email equal to the Google account address can sign in. The role comes from the database, a blocked user cannot sign in, and the application's two-factor code is not requested.

**What is needed in Google.** In the Google Cloud Console (a project in your Workspace organization), choose the **Internal** type on the consent screen, then create an OAuth client of type **Web application** and set the application address in "Authorized redirect URIs" exactly as users open it, for example `https://apps.example.com/`. The address must be on a domain with HTTPS: Google does not allow redirects to IP addresses. The Internal type admits only accounts of your Workspace organization; for accounts from other organizations the External type is needed (then the `google_domains` list and the user's presence in the database act as the restriction).

```r
settings <- aa_settings(
  google_enabled       = TRUE,
  google_client_id     = Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"),
  google_client_secret = Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET"),   # keep the secret outside the repository
  google_redirect_uri  = "https://apps.example.com/",
  google_domains       = c("example.com", "example.net"),            # allowed organization domains
  password_login       = TRUE                                        # FALSE: Google only (requires google_enabled)
)
```

After that the application changes nothing: `aa_auth_ui()` and `aa_auth_server()` show the button and handle the return from Google themselves.

**The application is opened at several addresses** (for example, both by IP and by domain). Google returns the user only to `google_redirect_uri`, while the sign-in `state` is stored in the cookie of the address where sign-in was started (cookies for an IP and for a domain are different). Therefore, on a page with a different address the "Sign in with Google" button redirects to the return address, and sign-in starts there on its own (the `?google=1` parameter, no second click needed). Password login and cookie auto-login work independently on each address, and nothing needs to be configured. The `login_success` event arrives with the value `google`, and failures arrive as the `google_login_failed` event (the reason and email in `value`: `no_user`, `blocked`, `domain`, `bad_browser`, and others), while the user is shown a generic text. For sign-in the user must have an email set (`aa_set_email()` or the user card).

`password_login = FALSE` hides the password form and the "Forgot your password?" link, and password login attempts are rejected on the server. Before disabling the password, make sure at least one administrator has an email set and Google sign-in works for them: otherwise there will be no way to sign in after disabling.

# A different database

By default the application opens a SQLite file. For DuckDB, MySQL / MariaDB, or PostgreSQL, pass `aa_session_connection()` a function that opens the connection (`db_path` is then not needed); the connection is closed together with the session:

```r
conn <- aa_session_connection(
  prepare = TRUE, settings = settings,
  connect = function() DBI::dbConnect(
    RPostgres::Postgres(),
    host = "db.example.com", dbname = "app", user = "app",
    password = Sys.getenv("APP_DB_PASSWORD")
  )
)
```

The rest of the application code (`aa_auth_server()`, `aa_users_server()`, `aa_can()`) does not change. The driver is installed separately: `RMariaDB`, `RPostgres`, or `duckdb`. Other databases (including BigQuery) are rejected with the `appauth_error_connection` error. If the application opens the connection itself, pass it to the package functions as is: the package identifies the database by the connection class.

# Texts

All interface texts and messages are available in English and Russian (English is the default); any string can be replaced.

```{r}
length(aa_text_keys())
texts <- aa_texts(login_button = "Log in", login_title = "Team sign-in")
texts$login_button

aa_text(texts, "locked", 15)          # value substitution: %d, %s
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
settings <- aa_settings(texts = aa_texts(login_title = "Reports portal"))

# Russian interface: aa_texts("ru")
settings_ru <- aa_settings(texts = aa_texts("ru"))
```

The list of keys: `aa_text_keys()`. An unknown key or an empty value raises an error immediately instead of a silently empty label in the interface.

# Appearance

`aa_app_head()` attaches the styles and the script. Colors are changed with CSS variables, which must be overridden **after** `aa_app_head()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ui <- fluidPage(
  aa_app_head(),
  tags$style(HTML(":root { --aa-primary: #0d9488; --aa-primary-hover: #0f766e; }")),
  ...
)
```

| Variable | What it colors |
| --- | --- |
| `--aa-primary`, `--aa-primary-hover` | The sign-in button, field focus |
| `--aa-danger`, `--aa-warning` | Errors, highlighting of blocked and temporarily blocked rows |
| `--aa-bg`, `--aa-card-bg`, `--aa-card-border` | The background of the sign-in page and the card |
| `--aa-text`, `--aa-muted` | Text colors |
| `--aa-input-bg`, `--aa-input-border` | Input fields |

The light theme is enabled with the `aa-theme-light` class on `<body>` or on a parent. Table row highlighting is set with `!important`, since application themes often set the cell background with it.

The title and logo of the sign-in form: `aa_auth_server("auth", conn, title = "My service", logo = "logo.png")`, with the image from the `www` folder.

# Security parameters

| `aa_settings()` parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_failed_logins` | 5 | failures before a login is locked |
| `lockout_minutes` | 15 | counting window and lock duration |
| `max_failed_logins_per_minute` | 30 | overall limit of failures across all logins |
| `password_min`, `password_max` | 6, 128 | length of a new password |
| `password_policy` | `"warn"` | weak passwords: `"off"` do not check, `"warn"` accept with a warning, `"reject"` reject |
| `login_max` | 64 | login length |
| `autologin` | `TRUE` | auto-login by cookie |
| `session_days` | 30 | token lifetime |
| `session_check_seconds` | 30 | how often to check an open session |
| `attempts_retention_hours`, `token_retention_days` | 24, 30 | how long to keep attempts and expired tokens |
| `roles`, `admin_role` | `admin`, `user`, `viewer` / `admin` | roles |
| `must_change_default` | `TRUE` | the default administrator password is temporary |
| `reset_enabled` | `FALSE` | password recovery by email (requires `send_reset` and `reset_base_url`) |
| `reset_ttl_minutes` | 60 | lifetime of the link from the email |
| `reset_max_per_hour`, `reset_max_per_minute` | 3, 10 | email limit per user per hour and overall per minute |
| `totp_enabled` | `FALSE` | two-factor authentication (TOTP), voluntary; requires `totp_key` |
| `totp_key` | `NULL` | TOTP secret encryption key (a string of at least 16 characters), keep outside the database |
| `totp_issuer`, `totp_window` | `"appauth"`, 1 | name in the authenticator app, allowed clock drift in steps of 30 seconds |

It is convenient to keep settings in `config.yaml` and read them with `aa_settings_from_list()`: extra keys in the list are ignored, and the language and texts are set by a separate argument.

The auto-login cookie name is set by `aa_auth_server(cookie_name = ...)`. Applications on the same host need different names: cookies are not isolated by port.

# What remains with the application

The package deliberately does not take on:

* the permission matrix and its editor;
* log switches and the log itself;
* the set of tabs and application-specific checks (task names, paths, commands);
* additional user fields (department, projects): they live in the application's tables next to the package tables, and are shown in the card through a slot.

If the same enhancement was needed in three applications, that is a reason to move it into the package.
